teaching.causalExplanation: For that order to mean anything, the test has to be fair. Use the same acid concentration and volume, the same temperature, and pieces with about the same surface area. Rub each metal with sandpaper first, because many metals carry a thin coating of oxide that slows the reaction down. Then the only thing that changes is the metal. So what's the gas? A metal that reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid makes a salt and hydrogen. Magnesium plus two hydrochloric acid gives magnesium chloride plus hydrogen. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop, and your teacher does that test on a small sample, because hydrogen is flammable. Use dilute acid, small amounts, and safety glasses, in a well-ventilated room. Add iron to the line-up, and it bubbles slowly. Aluminium foil is a surprise. At first it hardly bubbles at all, so keep that in mind. From the acid test, the order is magnesium, zinc, iron, and copper last, because copper makes no hydrogen.

The answer, in order: compare metals fairly in the same reagent (1, 2); rank them by how vigorously they react with acid (3, 4), water (5) and oxygen (6), and by which metals they displace from solution (7 to 10); the rankings agree, so they combine into one series with hydrogen placed by the acid test (11); compare it with a standard series and explain any mismatch (12).
- **Opening frame (self-contained; does not depend on m3-v06).** Heading "How is the reactivity of various metals predicted?" (the syllabus inquiry question) with three beakers of clear dilute acid (`m5x-unsaturated-beaker-v1.png`, three copies at one scale, each tagged "dilute HCl") and small metal tags "Mg", "Zn", "Cu" above them; the six ticked reaction-type strips from m3-v05's final frame small at the top right, dimmed (they were built over m3-v02 to m3-v05, so they do not depend on m3-v06). - **The hook is a fair comparison (route start: concrete case).** Same acid, three metals, three responses (site's "Same acid ... different" idea, with the safe student metals). Reactivity is defined by the observation before any series is shown.
- **Fair test (Working Scientifically).** Same acid concentration and volume, same temperature, similar-sized pieces, surfaces cleaned with sandpaper because of oxide coatings. The sanding point sets up aluminium's mismatch in scene 12.
- **Four reagents, four rankings (route stop; `C3-IQ2-01` lists all four).** Acid: Mg > Zn > Fe, Cu no reaction (student practical). Water: K > Na > Ca > Mg (K and Na by teacher demonstration behind a screen or footage, m1-v15; Ca as a teacher demonstration; Mg barely reacts with cold water, reacts with steam). Oxygen: Mg (brilliant white light) > Fe (filings burn as sparks in a flame) > Cu (blackens only; m3-v04). Metal ions: displacement (student practical, spotting plate). Each ranking is drawn as a short strip; scene 11 merges them.
- **Displacement explained without redox language.** "Zinc has gone into solution as zinc ions, and copper ions have come out as copper metal"; "the metal that ends up as ions is the more reactive one". Electrons appear only in the handoff (scene 18), recalling m1-v19's "metals lose electrons to form positive ions"; m3-v08 explains why, m3-v09 names it redox.
- **Prediction (3 s, scene 9).** "How many solutions will copper react with?" Answer: none. The grid answer for all four follows in scene 10.
- **Hydrogen's place.** From the acid test: metals that made hydrogen sit above it, copper below (site "Insight"). Lead is not tested; the reference places it above hydrogen.
- **Secondary comparison (`C3-IQ2-02`; Revision 2, brief 182 finding 4).** The school reactivity series as published by the Royal Society of Chemistry (RSC reactivity-series worksheet, https://edu.rsc.org/download?ac=503118; it supports K > Na > Ca; elements not shown are omitted), named and cited on screen. It is an observed school-series convention, not an ordering by reduction potentials (author note f). The constructed order matches for K, Na, Ca, Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu. Pb, Ag and Au come from the reference (lead compounds toxic; silver and gold costly). Aluminium's mismatch is explained in one sentence (a thin, tough oxide layer keeps the acid off until it breaks down; site "Must Know"); m3-v08 owns the underlying tendency against the surface.
- **Memory aid (site mnemonic; see "Memory aid check"):** "Please Stop Calling Me A Zombie, I Like Having Copper Silverware Guaranteed." Plus the rule line (Revision 2, scoped) "Clean metal, these solutions: it displaces a metal below it, never one above."
- **Attempts (original wording, HSC style).** A1 (data to series, the syllabus skill): metals X, Y, Z with acid and displacement results; X > Y > Z, hydrogen between Y and Z; crossed "Z > Y > X" (counting "was displaced" as reactivity). - **Handoff (route next: `chem-y11-m3-v08`, "Why do metal-reactivity trends follow electron removal?").** Scene 18: in every reaction the metal became positive ions, by losing electrons (m1-v19); the most reactive metals sit at the far left and low down in the periodic table. Final frame: see "Opening frame and final frame".
- **Site notes (read 5 November; for root to log if accepted):**
  1. Lesson 7, "Common Error: The NESA activity series lists hydrogen (H) as a reference point" and "According to the NESA activity series", "Use the NESA activity series", "the specific NESA-approved order": NESA does not publish an activity series; the HSC Chemistry data sheet gives a table of standard reduction potentials. Suggest "the standard activity series (consistent with the reduction potentials on the HSC data sheet)".
  2. Lesson 7, `l07-displacement-reactions...`: "the more reactive metal has a greater tendency to form ions, so it 'takes' the electron-release role away from the less reactive metal's ions." The less reactive metal's ions do not release electrons; they gain them. Suggest "the more reactive metal gives electrons to the less reactive metal's ions, which become metal atoms."
  3. Lesson 7, reactions table, magnesium with cold water "Very slow (reacts with steam)" and the key term "Mg reacts with hot water": both are fair, but the two cells differ; suggest "very slow in cold water; faster in hot water; vigorous with steam" in both places.
  - Checked and correct: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu; Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu; Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag with net Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag; the drill's Ag < Cu < Fe < Zn < Na; first ionisation energies K 419, Mg 738, Na 496, Li 520 kJ mol⁻¹ and electronegativities K 0.82, Mg 1.31, Na 0.93, Li 0.98 (used by m3-v08, not here); Q3(b) 0.050 × 65.4 = 3.27 g; the mnemonic's letters match K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au.

- **Entry knowledge:** m1-v15 (alkali metals in water), m1-v19 (metals lose electrons to form positive ions), m3-v03 (spectators, net ionic), m3-v04 (magnesium and copper with oxygen), m3-v05 (salts).
- **Learner-visible vocabulary (plain meaning at first use):** reactivity (how readily a metal reacts, 1); fair test (only one thing changes, 2); displacement reaction (a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound, 7); activity series (metals listed from most to least reactive, 11); secondary source (data collected by others, for example a published table, 12).
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Explainer motion (coded unless a plate is named):** **bubble meter** (scenes 1, 3, 4: a small bar beside each acid beaker rises with the plate's bubbling: tall, medium, low, zero); **ranking strips** (scenes 4, 5, 6, 10: one short strip per reagent with metal tiles ordered left to right, labelled "acid", "water", "oxygen", "metal ions"); **ion lens** (scenes 7, 8: from m3-v03; on the zinc surface, grey Zn atoms leave as amber Zn²⁺ while blue Cu²⁺ arrive and become brown Cu atoms; violet SO₄²⁻ swim on with grey spectator tags); **displacement grid** (scenes 9, 10: on `p03-well-plate-white-tile-v1.png`, a coded 4 × 4 block: rows "Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu", columns "MgSO₄, ZnSO₄, FeSO₄, CuSO₄"; the diagonal greyed "same metal"; each well shows a coded dark deposit or nothing; a tally column counts reactions); **series merge** (scene 11: the four strips slide together and their tiles align into one series; a dashed "H" line drops in between Fe and Cu); **reference compare** (scene 12: the reference series slides in under ours; matching tiles join with ticks; Pb, Ag, Au tiles drop down from the reference with the tag "from the reference"; Al gets an amber link and an oxide-skin inset); `Countdown`, `QuestionCard`, `Chip` with `cross`, `PenArrow`, `HandText`, `KeyNotes`, `Heading`.
- **Colour key (continues m3-v03 to v05):** metal tiles in metal tones; metal ions amber; copper ions blue; spectators grey; hydrogen line dashed teal; "from our data" teal outline, "from the reference" grey outline; mismatch amber; crossed items red strike.
- **Board layout (Revision 2):** heading top left; the ranking strips stack at the right. Revision 1 kept the plates in a row on the left two thirds for scenes 1 to 6 (about 150 s). Revision 2 stages, each under about 43 s: the three beakers filling the frame (1); the fair-test card with a large sandpaper inset (2); the full-width equation with the splint plate (3); the five-beaker row (4); the trough set (5); the three oxygen plates (6); the zinc beaker large with the ion lens (7); the equation stack (8); the displacement grid with live tallies (9, 10); the series merge (11); the reference compare (12); the mnemonic card (13).
- **Colour roles (Revision 2, fixed for the whole video):** metal tiles in their metal tones; metal ions amber; Cu²⁺ blue; hydrogen line teal dashed; our data teal outlines; reference grey outlines; surface-layer effects amber; framed answers in a dark-ink box with a green tick; crossed mistakes red strike plus a red hand tag; hand-font teacher tags take the colour of the item they mark; method and safety tags grey.
- **Type sizes (Revision 2, 1080p):** the current equation line at least 44 px (48 px); live grid tallies about 52 px; strip tiles 40 px; supporting lines 30 to 36 px; hand-font tags 34 to 40 px; nothing a student must read below 26 px. All text above the bottom 12% of the frame.
- **Simulation (Revision 2): the grid counter (scene 10).** A live readout on the core idea (the more solutions a metal displaces, the more reactive it is): as each well of the coded 4 × 4 grid shows a new metal deposit or stays clear, that row's live tally (52 px) climbs, and the ranking strip beside the grid re-sorts itself after each row, ending at Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu.

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) Acid test: typically 1 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid (or 0.5 to 2 mol L⁻¹, as the school's risk assessment sets), small pieces of similar mass or surface area; concentration not stated in learner copy ("dilute"). Iron reacts slowly (Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂); lead reacts very slowly (insoluble PbCl₂ coating) and is not used by students.
(b) Water: K and Na with cold water are teacher demonstrations behind a screen or footage (site; m1-v15); calcium with cold water is shown only as a teacher demonstration under the school's approved method or as checked secondary footage (Revision 2, brief 182 finding 5: the public NSW appendix confirms calcium reacts with atmospheric moisture and gives storage advice, but does not approve this exact trough demonstration); it is commonly a teacher demonstration (Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂; the water turns slightly cloudy); magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water, faster with hot water, vigorously with steam (Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂). Science check to confirm the calcium wording against current NSW school guidance.
(c) Oxygen: magnesium ribbon burns with a brilliant white light (never look straight at it, m3-v04); iron filings sprinkled into a Bunsen flame burn as sparks (a common teacher demonstration; the product is mainly Fe₃O₄, not stated); copper blackens without flame (2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO, m3-v04). Zinc powder burns but is not shown.
(d) Displacement grid (expected results): Mg displaces Zn, Fe, Cu (3); Zn displaces Fe, Cu (2); Fe displaces Cu (1); Cu displaces none (0). Iron(II) sulfate solution oxidises in air (yellow-brown); use freshly made solution (not stated in learner copy). Magnesium in some salt solutions also gives a little hydrogen; the deposit is the observation.
(e) Aluminium: the oxide layer (Al₂O₃) is a few nanometres thick and re-forms quickly; in dilute HCl the reaction starts slowly, then speeds up as chloride attacks the layer. m3-v08 owns "surface passivation against underlying tendency" (route).
(f) Secondary source (Revision 2): the RSC school reactivity series (cited above) is an observed order from reactions with water and acid. It is not the order of standard reduction potentials for Na and Ca: the HSC data sheet gives E°(Ca²⁺/Ca) = −2.87 V and E°(Na⁺/Na) = −2.71 V, which would put Ca above Na. The video follows the school series and teaches no E° values here (m3-v12 owns them). The RSC PDF returned HTTP 405 to direct retrieval; the order was read from indexed publisher text, so no visual inspection of the table is claimed. Site note 1's "consistent with reduction potentials" needs the same qualification.
(g) A2: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag; the solution turns pale blue slowly; silver grows as grey or shiny crystals. Silver nitrate stains skin (m2-v15's control).
(h) Pronunciations: "zinc two plus", "copper two plus" spoken once each; "X", "Y", "Z" as letters.

Main question: *How can observations order metals by reactivity?*
Entry knowledge: m1-v15, m1-v19, m3-v03, m3-v04, m3-v05.

Handoff: chem-y11-m3-v08, why reactivity follows electron removal.

- **Opening frame (self-contained):** heading "How is the reactivity of various metals predicted?"; three `m5x-unsaturated-beaker-v1.png` copies at one scale, each tagged "dilute HCl", with metal tags "Mg", "Zn", "Cu" above; the six ticked reaction-type strips from m3-v05's final frame small and dimmed at the top right (Revision 3: the combustion strip carries the scoped wording "combustion: hydrocarbon + O₂ → H₂O + CO₂, CO or C; metal + O₂ → oxide"). Root may reconcile with m3-v06's final frame when it is designed; no narration depends on m3-v06.
- **Final frame (m3-v08 opens on it):** left, our series as a vertical strip (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au; teal outline for tested metals, grey for reference-only, dashed H line), with an arrow "more reactive" pointing up; right, a mini periodic table outline with the same metals' cells shaded by rank (darkest for K), a pen arrow "down a group" on Group 1 and "to the left" across period 3; under it the tag "every metal here formed positive ions: M → Mⁿ⁺ + electrons"; an amber chip "easier to remove electrons?"; the chip "Next: Why do metal-reactivity trends follow electron removal?".

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "How can observations order metals by reactivity?" The answer, in order: compare metals fairly in the same reagent (1, 2); rank them by how vigorously they react with acid (3, 4), water (5) and oxygen (6), and by which metals they displace from solution (7 to 10); the rankings agree, so they combine into one series with hydrogen placed by the acid test (11); compare it with a standard series and explain any mismatch (12).
- **Opening frame (self-contained; does not depend on m3-v06).** Heading "How is the reactivity of various metals predicted?" (the syllabus inquiry question) with three beakers of clear dilute acid (`m5x-unsaturated-beaker-v1.png`, three copies at one scale, each tagged "dilute HCl") and small metal tags "Mg", "Zn", "Cu" above them; the six ticked reaction-type strips from m3-v05's final frame small at the top right, dimmed (they were built over m3-v02 to m3-v05, so they do not depend on m3-v06). When m3-v06 is designed, root may reconcile its final frame with this one; v07's narration does not refer to v06.
- **The hook is a fair comparison (route start: concrete case).** Same acid, three metals, three responses (site's "Same acid ... different" idea, with the safe student metals). Reactivity is defined by the observation before any series is shown.
- **Fair test (Working Scientifically).** Same acid concentration and volume, same temperature, similar-sized pieces, surfaces cleaned with sandpaper because of oxide coatings. The sanding point sets up aluminium's mismatch in scene 12.
- **Four reagents, four rankings (route stop; `C3-IQ2-01` lists all four).** Acid: Mg > Zn > Fe, Cu no reaction (student practical). Water: K > Na > Ca > Mg (K and Na by teacher demonstration behind a screen or footage, m1-v15; Ca as a teacher demonstration; Mg barely reacts with cold water, reacts with steam). Oxygen: Mg (brilliant white light) > Fe (filings burn as sparks in a flame) > Cu (blackens only; m3-v04). Metal ions: displacement (student practical, spotting plate). Each ranking is drawn as a short strip; scene 11 merges them.
- **Displacement explained without redox language.** "Zinc has gone into solution as zinc ions, and copper ions have come out as copper metal"; "the metal that ends up as ions is the more reactive one". Electrons appear only in the handoff (scene 18), recalling m1-v19's "metals lose electrons to form positive ions"; m3-v08 explains why, m3-v09 names it redox.
- **Prediction (3 s, scene 9).** "How many solutions will copper react with?" Answer: none. The grid answer for all four follows in scene 10.
- **Hydrogen's place.** From the acid test: metals that made hydrogen sit above it, copper below (site "Insight"). Lead is not tested; the reference places it above hydrogen.
- **Secondary comparison (`C3-IQ2-02`; Revision 2, brief 182 finding 4).** The school reactivity series as published by the Royal Society of Chemistry (RSC reactivity-series worksheet, https://edu.rsc.org/download?ac=503118; it supports K > Na > Ca; elements not shown are omitted), named and cited on screen. It is an observed school-series convention, not an ordering by reduction potentials (author note f). The constructed order matches for K, Na, Ca, Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu. Pb, Ag and Au come from the reference (lead compounds toxic; silver and gold costly). Aluminium's mismatch is explained in one sentence (a thin, tough oxide layer keeps the acid off until it breaks down; site "Must Know"); m3-v08 owns the underlying tendency against the surface.
- **Memory aid (site mnemonic; see "Memory aid check"):** "Please Stop Calling Me A Zombie, I Like Having Copper Silverware Guaranteed." Plus the rule line (Revision 2, scoped) "Clean metal, these solutions: it displaces a metal below it, never one above."
- **Attempts (original wording, HSC style).** A1 (data to series, the syllabus skill): metals X, Y, Z with acid and displacement results; X > Y > Z, hydrogen between Y and Z; crossed "Z > Y > X" (counting "was displaced" as reactivity). A2 (prediction from the series; site worked example (b), new wording): copper wire in silver nitrate: Cu(s) + 2AgNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2Ag(s), silver crystals and a blue solution; crossed "no reaction, because copper is below hydrogen".
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. "Any two substances mixed will react" (7: copper in zinc sulfate, nothing; site Common Error); "aluminium is unreactive" (12, crossed chip); "Z first" (A1 crossed); "compare with hydrogen, not the metal ion" (A2 crossed).
- **Handoff (route next: `chem-y11-m3-v08`, "Why do metal-reactivity trends follow electron removal?").** Scene 18: in every reaction the metal became positive ions, by losing electrons (m1-v19); the most reactive metals sit at the far left and low down in the periodic table. Final frame: see "Opening frame and final frame".
- **Site notes (read 5 November; for root to log if accepted):**
  1. Lesson 7, "Common Error: The NESA activity series lists hydrogen (H) as a reference point" and "According to the NESA activity series", "Use the NESA activity series", "the specific NESA-approved order": NESA does not publish an activity series; the HSC Chemistry data sheet gives a table of standard reduction potentials. Suggest "the standard activity series (consistent with the reduction potentials on the HSC data sheet)".
  2. Lesson 7, `l07-displacement-reactions...`: "the more reactive metal has a greater tendency to form ions, so it 'takes' the electron-release role away from the less reactive metal's ions." The less reactive metal's ions do not release electrons; they gain them. Suggest "the more reactive metal gives electrons to the less reactive metal's ions, which become metal atoms."
  3. Lesson 7, reactions table, magnesium with cold water "Very slow (reacts with steam)" and the key term "Mg reacts with hot water": both are fair, but the two cells differ; suggest "very slow in cold water; faster in hot water; vigorous with steam" in both places.
  - Checked and correct: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu; Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu; Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag with net Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag; the drill's Ag < Cu < Fe < Zn < Na; first ionisation energies K 419, Mg 738, Na 496, Li 520 kJ mol⁻¹ and electronegativities K 0.82, Mg 1.31, Na 0.93, Li 0.98 (used by m3-v08, not here); Q3(b) 0.050 × 65.4 = 3.27 g; the mnemonic's letters match K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au.
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) the same reagent and conditions make the metal the only variable, so differences show reactivity (1, 2); (2) a metal reacting with acid makes a salt and hydrogen, so bubbles measure vigour (3, 4); (3) water and oxygen are gentler and harsher tests that stretch the ranking at the top and bottom (5, 6); (4) a more reactive metal goes into solution as ions and pushes a less reactive metal's ions out as metal, never the reverse (7, 8); (5) counting displacements ranks many metals at once (9, 10); (6) independent tests agree, so they make one series, and hydrogen is placed by which metals made it (11); (7) a surface coating can hide a metal's reactivity, so a mismatch with the reference has a cause (12).
- **Entry knowledge:** m1-v15 (alkali metals in water), m1-v19 (metals lose electrons to form positive ions), m3-v03 (spectators, net ionic), m3-v04 (magnesium and copper with oxygen), m3-v05 (salts).

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) Acid test: typically 1 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid (or 0.5 to 2 mol L⁻¹, as the school's risk assessment sets), small pieces of similar mass or surface area; concentration not stated in learner copy ("dilute"). Iron reacts slowly (Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂); lead reacts very slowly (insoluble PbCl₂ coating) and is not used by students.
(b) Water: K and Na with cold water are teacher demonstrations behind a screen or footage (site; m1-v15); calcium with cold water is shown only as a teacher demonstration under the school's approved method or as checked secondary footage (Revision 2, brief 182 finding 5: the public NSW appendix confirms calcium reacts with atmospheric moisture and gives storage advice, but does not approve this exact trough demonstration); it is commonly a teacher demonstration (Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂; the water turns slightly cloudy); magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water, faster with hot water, vigorously with steam (Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂). Science check to confirm the calcium wording against current NSW school guidance.
(c) Oxygen: magnesium ribbon burns with a brilliant white light (never look straight at it, m3-v04); iron filings sprinkled into a Bunsen flame burn as sparks (a common teacher demonstration; the product is mainly Fe₃O₄, not stated); copper blackens without flame (2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO, m3-v04). Zinc powder burns but is not shown.
(d) Displacement grid (expected results): Mg displaces Zn, Fe, Cu (3); Zn displaces Fe, Cu (2); Fe displaces Cu (1); Cu displaces none (0). Iron(II) sulfate solution oxidises in air (yellow-brown); use freshly made solution (not stated in learner copy). Magnesium in some salt solutions also gives a little hydrogen; the deposit is the observation.
(e) Aluminium: the oxide layer (Al₂O₃) is a few nanometres thick and re-forms quickly; in dilute HCl the reaction starts slowly, then speeds up as chloride attacks the layer. m3-v08 owns "surface passivation against underlying tendency" (route).
(f) Secondary source (Revision 2): the RSC school reactivity series (cited above) is an observed order from reactions with water and acid. It is not the order of standard reduction potentials for Na and Ca: the HSC data sheet gives E°(Ca²⁺/Ca) = −2.87 V and E°(Na⁺/Na) = −2.71 V, which would put Ca above Na. The video follows the school series and teaches no E° values here (m3-v12 owns them). The RSC PDF returned HTTP 405 to direct retrieval; the order was read from indexed publisher text, so no visual inspection of the table is claimed. Site note 1's "consistent with reduction potentials" needs the same qualification.
(g) A2: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag; the solution turns pale blue slowly; silver grows as grey or shiny crystals. Silver nitrate stains skin (m2-v15's control).
(h) Pronunciations: "zinc two plus", "copper two plus" spoken once each; "X", "Y", "Z" as letters.

Main question: *How can observations order metals by reactivity?*
Entry knowledge: m1-v15, m1-v19, m3-v03, m3-v04, m3-v05.
Stops after: fair comparisons in acid, water, oxygen and metal-ion solutions; four rankings combined into one series with hydrogen placed; comparison with a standard series, untested metals filled in and aluminium's mismatch explained. No electron-removal explanation, no redox language.
Handoff: chem-y11-m3-v08, why reactivity follows electron removal.
